profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at an academic medical center between the clinical lead and the trial statistician for a Phase II oncology study evaluating whether to incorporate a conservative Bayesian design using external evidence from prior PD-1 combination studies. They need to plan the design workup for a protocol concept note due to the internal development committee next week. The agenda is to align on what 'conservative' means for the design package, decide what external evidence will feed the design prior, assign who will draft the operating-characteristics summary, and set the timeline for delivering a go/no-go recommendation framework. The expected outcome is a shared plan for producing a design brief, sample size recommendation, and summary of stopping rules for the committee.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Early-phase solid tumor development, protocol strategy, clinical interpretation of efficacy and futility signals
members.background: A thoracic oncologist who has led several Phase Ib/II immunotherapy programs and regularly presents concepts to the institutional development committee.
members.private_state: She wants a design that looks appropriately cautious to the committee while still preserving a realistic chance of advancing the program; she is especially concerned about avoiding an appearance that historical evidence is being used too aggressively.
hidden_assumptions: A 'conservative prior' means the prior should be weaker than the planned trial evidence so the final recommendation is visibly driven by the new study.
The 'external evidence set' naturally refers only to studies in the same tumor type and line of therapy as the planned trial, because broader borrowing would be hard to defend clinically.
A 'go/no-go package' should include a clinically interpretable recommendation memo with scenario-based conclusions, not just simulation outputs.

When discussing 'futility,' the team is talking about an explicit early non-binding futility look that can support stopping for lack of promise, since negative evidence from efficacy monitoring alone is usually insufficient.

members.name: Dr. Aaron Shah
members.expertise: Bayesian adaptive design, operating-characteristics simulation, group sequential methods for oncology trials
members.background: A senior trial statistician who has designed Bayesian early-phase studies for industry-sponsored and investigator-initiated oncology programs.
members.private_state: He wants to deliver an efficient design proposal quickly and assumes the committee mainly needs a statistically defensible framework rather than a polished clinical decision memo; he is also trying to reuse a prior elicitation template from a recent immunotherapy program.
hidden_assumptions: A 'conservative prior' means using a skeptical or conflict-robust prior distribution, even if the operating characteristics are informed by a fairly broad external evidence base.
The 'external evidence set' can reasonably include adjacent tumor types and mechanistically similar PD-1 combination studies if they inform the discrete design prior conservatively.
A 'go/no-go package' is satisfied by a technical design deck containing assumptions, simulations, and decision thresholds; clinical narrative can be added later if needed.
When discussing 'futility,' everyone understands this as part of the standard group sequential design framework and not necessarily as a separately specified non-binding futility boundary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use a 'conservative prior' for the Phase II design.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the prior must be subordinate to the primary trial outcome, with sample size chosen so the trial's operating characteristics are stronger than the prior and visibly protect against prior-data conflict.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the prior distribution itself should be skeptical or robustified, while still allowing external evidence to play a substantial role in the design workup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and both are positively disposed toward caution, so each hears confirmation of their own technical interpretation without expecting the other to mean something different.

misalignment_points.topic: Which studies count as the external evidence set
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to building the design prior from the 'external evidence set' or 'the prior studies.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking only of prior studies in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, second-line setting, with endpoints comparable to the planned trial.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a broader basket including melanoma and head-and-neck PD-1 combination studies plus one first-line NSCLC study, because the borrowing is only for design calibration rather than direct analysis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume the phrase 'external evidence' has an obvious domain-specific boundary, and because they are planning rather than reviewing individual citations, the exact inclusion boundary never gets enumerated.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they need a 'go/no-go package' for the committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the package is complete only if it contains a clinically framed recommendation, plain-language rationale about equipoise imbalance, and implications under optimistic and pessimistic scenarios.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the package is complete once the technical design brief includes sample size, simulated operating characteristics, and threshold tables supporting a decision framework.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In development meetings, 'package' often functions as shorthand for whatever each discipline usually contributes, so each assumes the other's deliverable expectations are naturally nested within their own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the design should include 'futility' so the study can stop early if it is not promising.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a distinct non-binding futility rule to be planned explicitly, because she assumes efficacy boundaries alone provide negligible negative evidence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to rely mainly on the existing group sequential monitoring structure and discuss lack of crossing efficacy as the practical manifestation of futility unless separately requested.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse early stopping for lack of promise, and procedural details of how futility is operationalized feel like technical implementation rather than a separate planning issue worth unpacking.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to look disciplined in front of the development committee. If we use a conservative prior, it has to be obviously subordinate to the trial itself, otherwise it will look like we're backfilling enthusiasm from old PD-1 studies. And the go/no-go package can't just be a stats deck; I need something I can stand behind clinically when they ask what we would actually recommend under different outcomes.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. For next week's concept note, I'd like us to put forward a conservative Bayesian approach that the committee will see as cautious but still practical, and I'd like us aligned on what goes into the go/no-go package.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds straightforward. I can reuse the prior elicitation framework from the recent immunotherapy program, make the prior conservative, and show the operating characteristics cleanly. For the committee, a technical go/no-go package with assumptions, thresholds, and simulation outputs should be enough to get the concept through this stage.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I think the cleanest way is to organize it around a conservative prior, a set of operating-characteristics simulations, and a go/no-go package for the development committee.

turns.inner_thought: I want the external evidence set kept tight: second-line metastatic NSCLC, comparable endpoints, studies a clinician on the committee would recognize as truly relevant. If it gets broader than that, I'll spend the whole meeting defending why those studies belong.
turns.utterance: That works. On the prior, I want it anchored in the external evidence set that's most relevant to the planned second-line lung population, so the overall recommendation stays clinically defensible.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're on the same page about using the external evidence set. I can pull the prior studies from the recent PD-1 combination work quickly, including the adjacent programs that help stabilize the calibration. Since this is for design prior construction rather than direct borrowing in the final analysis, that's a reasonable and conservative basis.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can pull the prior studies fairly quickly from the recent PD-1 combination programs and discretize that into a design prior for calibration.

turns.inner_thought: The key is that when the committee looks at this, they can see the recommendation is driven by the new Phase II data, not by the prior. The sample size and design have to make that visible. I don't want anyone saying we talked ourselves into a signal before we ran the study.
turns.utterance: Good. I also want to be sure the primary trial outcome is stronger than the prior, so it's clear the new study is carrying the weight of the decision.

turns.inner_thought: Makes sense—she wants something appropriately cautious. I'll make the prior conservative and conflict-robust, then see what sample size gives acceptable type of behavior across the scenarios. If the prior is skeptical enough, that should address any concern about overreliance on historical information.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll make the prior conservative and conflict-robust, and then check what sample size gives us acceptable operating characteristics.

turns.inner_thought: When I say go/no-go package, I need more than plots and tables. I need something that shows, in plain terms, how this behaves in good and bad cases and how it informs a clinically sensible recommendation, especially around equipoise. But Aaron usually gives strong technical material, so maybe I can layer the clinical framing on top once I see it.
turns.utterance: And for the go/no-go package, I'd like it to show clearly how the design behaves under favorable and unfavorable scenarios, and how it supports the clinical equipoise discussion.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine—I can give her scenario-based simulation tables and threshold summaries. That should cover favorable and unfavorable cases well enough, and if she wants narrative later, she can add it. I should be able to turn this around fast if I keep the deliverable to the design deck.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can have a package by Monday with simulation tables, threshold summaries, and a couple of recommended sample size options.

turns.inner_thought: One thing I do not want is to discover too late that 'futility' was only implied. In these settings, standard efficacy monitoring rarely gives enough negative signal to justify stopping, so I need an explicit early non-binding futility look built in. I don't think I need to spell that out because that's usually what we mean when we say futility.
turns.utterance: One other thing: because confirmatory-style efficacy monitoring often gives very little negative evidence, I do want futility built in so the study can stop early if it's not promising.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. I can handle futility within the interim monitoring framework. The group sequential structure will cover the practical need here, and if the study isn't doing enough at interim, that will come through in the monitoring plan. No need to overcomplicate it unless she asks for a separate boundary later.
turns.utterance: Agreed, futility is important. I'll incorporate that into the monitoring framework when I lay out the interim design.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take responsibility for the clinical recommendation language, because that's what the committee will actually react to. Once Aaron sends the design brief, I can wrap it into a recommendation memo with scenario-based conclusions and context about why we'd continue or stop.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll draft the clinical context for the committee, and if you send me the design brief, I can fold it into the recommendation.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll compile the prior studies from the external evidence set, run the calibration, and package the technical materials with the interim monitoring plan. That should be enough for committee review, and Lena can layer on whatever clinical narrative she wants.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll compile the prior studies, run the calibration, and send over the go/no-go package with the interim plan by Monday so it's ready for committee review.
